input.candidate_text:
Let \(G\) and \(H\) be nonabelian groups of order \(21\). By Sylow's theorems, the number of Sylow \(7\)-subgroups divides \(3\) and is congruent to \(1\pmod 7\), so each group has a unique, hence normal, Sylow \(7\)-subgroup. Write these as \(B=\langle b\rangle\le G\) and \(D=\langle d\rangle\le H\).

By Cauchy's theorem, choose elements \(a\in G\) and \(c\in H\) of order \(3\). Since \(\langle a\rangle\cap B=\{e\}\) and their orders multiply to \(21\), \(G=B\langle a\rangle\). Similarly, \(H=D\langle c\rangle\).

Normality of \(B\) gives \(aba^{-1}=b^i\) for some \(i\in(\mathbb Z/7\mathbb Z)^\times\). Because \(a^3=e\),
\[
b=a^3ba^{-3}=b^{i^3},
\]
so \(i^3\equiv1\pmod 7\). The solutions are \(i=1,2,4\). If \(i=1\), then \(a\) and \(b\) commute; since they generate \(G\), this would make \(G\) abelian. Thus \(i=2\) or \(4\). Replacing \(a\) by \(a^{-1}\) when necessary changes exponent \(4\) to its inverse \(2\pmod 7\). Hence we may choose \(a\) so that
\[
aba^{-1}=b^2.
\]
Likewise, we may choose \(c\) so that \(cdc^{-1}=d^2\).

Every element of \(G\) has a unique expression \(b^j a^r\), where \(0\le j<7\) and \(0\le r<3\). The analogous statement holds in \(H\). Define
\[
\phi(b^j a^r)=d^j c^r.
\]
This is therefore a well-defined bijection. Moreover,
\[
(b^j a^r)(b^k a^s)=b^{j+2^r k}a^{r+s},
\]
with exponents taken modulo \(7\) and \(3\), respectively. Since the identical multiplication formula holds for \(d^j c^r\), the map \(\phi\) is a homomorphism. Consequently \(\phi\) is an isomorphism, so any two nonabelian groups of order \(21\) are isomorphic.

problem.theorem: Prove that any two nonabelian groups of order 21 are isomorphic.
